subject: Linear Algebra (GATE DA)
weightagePercent: 8-13% of total 100 marks (≈8-13 marks; roughly 5-8 of the 55 core questions)
difficulty: Moderate-to-High. Computationally mechanical once formulas are internalized (eigenvalues, rank, LU), but GATE DA's syllabus is explicitly broader than GATE-CS Linear Algebra — it adds projection/orthogonal/idempotent/partition matrices, quadratic forms, and SVD, none of which are core to a standard CS-track linear algebra course. These "extra" topics are where most marks are lost by candidates who reuse old GATE-CS notes. NAT-format questions (Gaussian elimination, rank, eigenvalue computation) add time pressure and no partial credit for arithmetic slips.
pyqTrendByYear: Precise official topic-tagging doesn't exist for any year (GATE never publishes it), so these are the best available reconstructions: 2024 ≈ 6 questions / 10 marks (~10% of total) — this is the widely-mirrored GeeksforGeeks-style coaching estimate, internally consistent and summing correctly to 65Q/100M across all subjects. 2025 ≈ 8 questions / 12 marks (~12%) — this figure comes from the digest's own author personally classifying all 55 core GATE DA 2025 questions against the official syllabus PDF (higher confidence than a generic coaching table, though still a judgment call at the margins, e.g. whether a Gaussian-elimination-complexity question is "Linear Algebra" or "Programming/Algorithms"). 2026: no single reliable breakdown exists; my own targeted searches this session found conflicting unofficial estimates ranging from a low ~5-6Q/8-10M (~8%) to vaguer "15-20% of core" framings on different coaching pages, with one source's numbers looking like a possible cross-paper data error (implausibly low 2-3 total marks) — net read is that 2026 likely reverted toward the 2024 level (~8-10%) after 2025's slightly elevated share. Style also drifted: 2025's official paper (per the digest) included a purely conceptual PCA/eigenvalue question (Q60, no computation required) alongside heavier applied-geometry items, suggesting a trend toward blending LA with ML application rather than pure textbook computation — but with only 3 editions this is suggestive, not proven.
expected2027: Medium confidence: expect Linear Algebra to hold steady at roughly 8-13% of total marks (5-8 questions), because all three editions to date have fallen in or near that band and the official syllabus wording has been byte-for-byte identical for 2024/2025/2026 with no signal of change (per the syllabus_pattern digest entry). High confidence sub-prediction: SVD and eigenvalue/eigenvector questions will reappear in 2027, since both are explicitly named in the syllabus and both feed directly into the Machine Learning section's PCA topic — coaching sources this session independently converged on SVD as "the most important LA topic, do not skip it." Low confidence: whether 2027 will bring more standalone LA questions or more LA-inside-ML hybrid questions (e.g., "PCA via eigendecomposition" style items straddling both syllabus sections) — the n=3 sample is too small and no GATE 2027 brochure/syllabus has been published yet (per the digest's syllabus_pattern entry, as of 17 Jul 2026) to call this confidently.
priorityForTopRank: High. For a time-constrained working professional targeting AIR 50-200, Linear Algebra offers unusually good ROI: (1) it is almost purely mechanical/formulaic once mastered, unlike Probability & Statistics or AI which require more scenario judgment; (2) at ~8-13% direct weightage it is comparable to Machine Learning or AI alone, but it also silently underpins ML questions (PCA=SVD/eigendecomposition, linear/ridge regression normal equations, SVM margin geometry) and parts of Calculus & Optimization — so mastering it yields marks in at least two syllabus sections; (3) the "extra" DA-specific topics (projection/orthogonal/idempotent/partition matrices, quadratic forms, SVD) are a known blind spot for candidates who only studied GATE-CS-style linear algebra, meaning strong prep here is a real differentiator against the broader applicant pool rather than a commodity skill everyone already has. Recommended allocation: front-load this subject early in a study plan (it has few prerequisites beyond high-school algebra) and revisit it again right before the exam paired with the ML PCA/SVM topics for combined-topic recall.
cheatSheet: Rank-nullity theorem: rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, where n = number of columns of A (dim of domain)
Eigenvalues from det(A − λI) = 0; trace(A) = Σλ_i; det(A) = Πλ_i — fast sanity checks on any eigenvalue computation
Symmetric matrices: always have real eigenvalues and an orthogonal eigenvector basis (spectral theorem) — this is why PCA works on covariance matrices
Orthogonal matrix Q: QᵀQ = I = QQᵀ; preserves lengths/angles; all eigenvalues satisfy |λ| = 1
Idempotent matrix: A² = A ⇒ eigenvalues ∈ {0, 1} only; a projection matrix is idempotent AND symmetric
Projection matrix onto column space of A: P = A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ — appears in linear regression's normal equations (OLS hat matrix)
SVD: A = UΣVᵀ; singular values σ_i = √(eigenvalues of AᵀA) = √(eigenvalues of AAᵀ); U's columns = eigenvectors of AAᵀ, V's columns = eigenvectors of AᵀA
SVD ↔ PCA link: PCA = eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix = SVD of the (mean-centered) data matrix — a near-guaranteed cross-topic exam link
A matrix is diagonalizable iff it has n linearly independent eigenvectors (always true if all n eigenvalues are distinct)
Quadratic form xᵀAx is positive definite iff all eigenvalues of (symmetric) A are > 0, equivalently all leading principal minors are > 0
LU decomposition = encoding of Gaussian elimination steps (L = multipliers used, U = row-echelon result); watch for when pivoting/row-swaps are needed (no clean LU without a permutation matrix P)
Partition/block matrix multiplication follows normal matrix multiplication rules block-by-block, provided block dimensions are conformable
Determinant properties: det(AB) = det(A)det(B); a row swap flips sign; a row of zeros ⇒ det = 0; det(Aᵀ) = det(A)
Gaussian elimination row-reduces to find rank quickly: rank = number of non-zero rows in row-echelon form
commonMistakes: Reusing old GATE-CS linear algebra notes/courses, which skip DA-specific syllabus items — projection, orthogonal, idempotent, and partition matrices, and quadratic forms — leaving easy marks on the table

Treating SVD as optional/skippable because it isn't emphasized in generic engineering-math courses, despite being explicitly named in the official syllabus every year since 2024 and repeatedly flagged by coaching sources as the single most important LA topic
Confusing eigenvalues with singular values (they coincide only for symmetric positive semi-definite matrices) — a frequently-cited specific trap

Confusing algebraic multiplicity (multiplicity of λ as a root of the characteristic polynomial) with geometric multiplicity (dimension of the eigenspace) — these differ for defective/non-diagonalizable matrices
Losing NAT marks to arithmetic slips under time pressure during Gaussian elimination or eigenvalue computation — there is no partial credit on NAT, so a single sign error zeroes the question
Over-investing prep time in numerical-methods-style iterative eigenvalue/rank algorithms that are out of scope for GATE DA's syllabus, at the expense of the syllabus's actual named topics

Not connecting Linear Algebra prep to the Machine Learning section (PCA, SVM geometry, regression normal equations) — missing 'free' cross-topic marks and under-preparing for hybrid LA+ML questions like 2025's conceptual PCA/eigenvalue item

Memorizing formulas for special matrices (idempotent, orthogonal, projection) without practicing quickly identifying which type a given matrix is from its stated properties — a recurring GATE DA question pattern per coaching-source review
